reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: The plantar plate is the fibrocartilaginous plantar stabiliser of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joint, and its attrition or tear causes pain and progressive instability
The second toe is most commonly affected, and patients describe plantar pain at the base of the toe, often with a feeling of walking on a lump and swelling of the joint
The modified drawer (Lachman-type) test, in which dorsal translation of the proximal phalanx on the metatarsal head reproduces pain and shows increased laxity, is the key clinical sign
Progressive insufficiency leads to dorsal and medial drift of the toe, producing the crossover toe deformity in which the second toe overrides the hallux
The V-sign, a widening gap between the second and third toes, is an early indicator of medial deviation from plantar plate failure
Ultrasound and MRI are the most useful investigations to confirm the tear and grade its severity, while weight-bearing radiographs assess alignment and exclude other causes
Distinguish it from interdigital neuroma, which typically causes interspace rather than joint pain and lacks the instability signs

Early management is conservative with metatarsal offloading orthoses, toe strapping or taping to hold the toe plantarward, stiff-soled footwear, and activity modification, with plantar plate repair or reconstruction and associated deformity correction reserved for failed cases
reference.pathophysiology: The plantar plate is a thick fibrocartilaginous structure on the plantar surface of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joint that resists dorsiflexion and hyperextension and, together with the collateral ligaments, provides the main static stability of the joint. Chronic dorsiflexion overload, as occurs with a long metatarsal, hallux valgus that crowds the second toe, high-heeled footwear, or inflammatory disease, produces cumulative attritional injury that weakens and eventually tears the plate, usually near its insertion into the base of the proximal phalanx. As the plantar restraint fails, the proximal phalanx drifts dorsally and the toe becomes unstable, and asymmetrical involvement of the collateral ligaments allows medial deviation, giving the characteristic crossover second toe that overrides the hallux. Loss of the plantar cushioning contributes to metatarsalgia beneath the involved head. The process is typically gradual and degenerative rather than the result of a single acute event.
additionalDifferentials: Freiberg's infraction of the metatarsal head
Metatarsophalangeal joint synovitis from inflammatory arthritis
Hammer or claw toe deformity from other mechanisms
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including the modified drawer test and inspection for crossover deformity and the V-sign
Weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess metatarsal length, alignment, and toe position
Ultrasound to visualise the plantar plate and dynamic instability
MRI to confirm and grade the tear and assess collateral ligament involvement
Assessment for associated hallux valgus and metatarsal length abnormality
Pedobarography to characterise forefoot overload where relevant
Inflammatory markers and serology if a synovitic or inflammatory cause is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dorsal dislocation of the toe with fixed crossover deformity
Symmetrical or multiple joint synovitis suggesting underlying inflammatory arthritis
Focal bony tenderness suggesting a coexisting stress fracture
A hot, swollen joint raising the possibility of septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy
Neurovascular compromise of the drifting toe
reference.prognosis: Early and partial tears often stabilise or improve with offloading, taping, and footwear modification, though these measures control symptoms rather than heal the plate. Once fixed deformity or dislocation develops, conservative treatment is less effective and surgical plantar plate repair or reconstruction with deformity correction is required; results are generally good but some residual stiffness, recurrence, or floating toe may occur.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as an interdigital neuroma and treating the wrong structure
Failing to perform the drawer test and missing early instability before fixed deformity develops
Overlooking associated hallux valgus or a long metatarsal that drives recurrence if uncorrected
Assuming conservative treatment will heal a complete tear rather than merely control symptoms
Missing an inflammatory arthropathy underlying multiple-joint synovitis
